description_full: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. operates as a semiconductor company internationally. It operates in three segments: Data Center, Client and Gaming, and Embedded. The company offers artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators, microprocessors, and graphics processing units (GPUs) as standalone devices or as incorporated into accelerated processing units, chipsets, and data center and professional GPUs; and embedded processors and semi-custom system-on-chip (SoC) products, microprocessor and SoC development services and technology, data processing units, field programmable gate arrays (FPGA), system on modules, AI network interface cards, and adaptive SoC products. It provides processors under the AMD Ryzen, AMD Ryzen AI, AMD Ryzen PRO, AMD Ryzen Threadripper, AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO, AMD Athlon, and AMD PRO A-Series brands; graphics under the AMD Radeon graphics and AMD Embedded Radeon graphics; professional graphics under the AMD Radeon Pro graphics brand; and AI and general-purpose compute infrastructure for hyperscale providers. The company offers data center graphics under the AMD Instinct accelerators and Radeon PRO V-series brands; server microprocessors under the AMD EPYC brand; low power solutions under the AMD Athlon, AMD Geode, AMD Ryzen, AMD EPYC, and AMD R-Series and G-Series brands; FPGA products under the Virtex-6, Virtex-7, Virtex UltraScale+, Kintex-7, Kintex UltraScale, Kintex UltraScale+, Artix-7, Artix UltraScale+, Spartan-6, and Spartan-7 brands; adaptive SOCs under the Zynq-7000, Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC, Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoCs, Versal HBM, Versal Premium, Versal Prime, Versal AI Core, Versal AI Edge, Vitis, and Vivado brands; and compute and network acceleration board products under the Alveo and Pensando brands. It serves original equipment and design manufacturers, public cloud service providers, system integrators, distributors, and add-in-board manufacturers. The company was incorporated in 1969 and is headquartered in Santa Clara, California.

financial_summary: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. is a mega-cap technology business with a $875.9B market cap on $34.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and +24% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 44%.

The business throws off $6.7B in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.78× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 28× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 11% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 144% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 19% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 73% and a beta of 1.53, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.96 vs 5y 1.95), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $10.9B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash, 63% in the 2022 bear market and 78% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $51.62 (margin of safety -935%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 33%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $32.72 to $84.94 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 114.1 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 85.6 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 130.1 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 173% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 49 covering analysts target $658 on average, 23% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 11.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 3.38).
It runs a 44% gross margin and converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow, or 15% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.78x.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 23.4% of revenue on R&D and 4.7% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $6.5B (1% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 38.7, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 171 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.6% over 3 years, 28.8% over 5 years and 24.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 25%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 4.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 54.0% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.01, a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 82%.
Capex runs 1.9x depreciation (2.8% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 44, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 77%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (85 sales, net $116.3M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.2% (0.2% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 6.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 31,000 employees, each generates about $1.1M of revenue, 3.0x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 11.8% a year across its filed history.
